extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Latin literature, translators, and textual editors
extracted.subtask_description: Annotated critical edition and commentary for Horace's Epistles that guides translation, textual emendation, explanation of allusions, and literary interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report textual variants and editorial sigla
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate manuscript readings, editorial omissions, and alternative readings using sigla (e.g., E, aM, R, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the variant form, mark omissions (e.g., 'et omitted aMS'), record conjectural readings and which editors accept them (e.g., 'Bentley conjecture', 'accepted by Lachmann, Kiessling, Holder'), and note majority/editorial preference (e.g., 'most editors exterruit utrumque').

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve traditional text unless strong grounds for emendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain the traditional/traditional_ms reading where plausible rather than replacing it with conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state when the traditional text should be kept (example: 'traditional text must be retained' about the fox/grain passage) and explain why an alternative is only conjectural or less plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify and cite conjectural emendations
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposing or adopting an emendation, attribute it and record its reception among editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name the conjecturer (e.g., 'Bentley'), note which later editors accepted or rejected it, and provide rationale or textual/metrical reasons for preferring the emendation (examples throughout the notes where conjectures and acceptances are recorded).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain obscure words, idioms, and variant interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide glosses for uncertain or archaic terms and record alternative meanings or scholarly opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss possible senses (e.g., 'pondera' as stepping-stones vs. 'weights on a shop-counter'), note scholarly conjectures, and mark interpretations as conjectural where appropriate. Include brief lexical or cultural explanations (e.g., 'cera refers to wax-covered tablets').

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide historical and intertextual identifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify persons, places, historical references, and parallels to other classical works mentioned or alluded to in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give short biographies or citations (e.g., 'For Lucullus see Plutarch's Lives; Lucullus, ch. 39'), point to relevant passages in other works (e.g., Od. ii. 601ff., Cic. Ad Att. vi.3), and explain relevance to the passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize key theme or 'key‑note' at head of poem/epistle
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin each piece of commentary with a concise statement of the poem's central idea or theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the 'key-note' in plain terms (example: 'Nil admirari ... is perhaps the one and only thing ... that can make a man happy'), then show how the following lines develop that theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map philosophical and technical terms to their cultural/philological equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain philosophical or foreign‑language concepts by giving parallels and source‑terms (e.g., Latin to Greek philosophical vocabulary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connect Latin phrases to Greek originals and philosophical schools (example: render 'nil admirari' in relation to Greek terms used by Pythagoras, Democritus, Stoics, Epicureans), and, when helpful, illustrate meaning with later quotations (e.g., Tennyson) or concise paraphrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace rhetorical and moral argument flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Outline the poem's argumentative structure and the moral or rhetorical moves the poet makes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize how the poet moves from premise to illustration to conclusion (e.g., claim that 'wise indifference' is clue to happiness, followed by examples of desire/fear, then practical counsels), and explicate individual illustrative anecdotes and their function in the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-reference line numbers and related passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide precise line references and cross-references to other poems, odes, satires, or classical passages cited in the commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite line numbers (e.g., '1–27'), refer to other works and line locations (e.g., 'cf. Od. iii. 21. 13 ff.'), and indicate where parallel usages or references inform interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record metrically or formally notable readings and obliquities
rubrics_metrics.description: Note when a reading affects sense or poetic form (e.g., meter, scansion, abruptness) and comment on the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag passages where variant readings alter cadence or rhetorical force, indicate if a form seems corrupt or metrically awkward, and discuss how emendation would restore expected formal properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer translation guidance: literal vs idiomatic choices
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating, indicate where a literal rendering would mislead and suggest idiomatic alternatives that preserve tone and rhetorical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide paraphrase and an idiomatic translation side‑by‑side in the notes (examples: translating cultural images like 'honeyed cakes' vs 'bread' and explaining the social contrast), and flag philosophically loaded words that need nuanced renderings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use illustrative exempla and scholiast tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ stories, scholiast commentary, and traditional anecdotes to illuminate meaning or usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include short narratives or scholia (e.g., the fox-and-weasel fable, accounts of Lucullus and the Cappadocian king), note their source, and explain how they support the poem's point or the editor's reading.
